candidates.title: Sealed-Bid Auction Lesson
candidates.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you bid against simulated rivals in first-price and second-price sealed auctions and see how shading your bid changes your profit.
candidates.pitch: You get a private value for an item (say a mug worth 60 play-dollars to you) and bid against four simulated rivals, first in a rising-price auction, then in sealed first-price and second-price versions. A slider shades your bid below or above your value and a profit curve, built from thousands of replayed rounds, shows that shading pays in the first-price auction and never pays in the second-price one. You leave knowing why the rule of the game, not good manners, makes honest bidding the best plan, and exactly when that stops being true.
candidates.firstMinute: The first frame already shows an ascending auction running: a price ladder climbs, rivals drop out, and a card says what the item is worth to you. You tap Drop out when the price reaches your value, see you won with a small profit, and see the same round replayed with a higher and a lower dropout point so you can see why leaving at your value was best.
conceptsToLearn: your value for an item is what it is worth to you; profit is value minus the price you pay
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. The ad-tech industry's 2019 switch from second-price to first-price auctions made bid shading a live topic, and nobody shows the arithmetic behind it.

purposeDetail.concept: In a sealed-bid second-price auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, so your own bid only decides whether you win, never what you pay; bidding your true value is therefore a dominant strategy when values are private. In a first-price auction you pay what you bid, so you shade below value; with n risk-neutral bidders whose values are independent and uniform on 0 to 1, the equilibrium bid is (n-1)/n of your value.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: It is usually taught as a theorem or as a one-line conclusion, so it sounds like an opinion. Few places let a learner try to cheat the rule and watch it fail, or show that the same honest bid is wrong under a different rule.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults, students of economics or computer science, and anyone who has argued about eBay, ad markets or spectrum sales.
prerequisites: subtracting a price from a value
misconceptions: Bidding below my value always saves me money, in any auction.
Honest bidding is a naive rule that leaves money on the table.
Honest bidding is best in every auction format, whatever the other rules or information.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: You drag your bid anywhere you like in the second-price auction, and the price you pay never moves until the exact point where you stop winning. The profit curve is flat across winning bids and drops off a cliff either side of your value, whereas the first-price curve has a hump below your value.
demos: Rung 1: a rising-price ladder auction with four simulated rivals; you choose when to drop out; the page replays the round with other dropout points.

Rung 2: sealed first-price round; type or drag a bid; the winner pays their own bid; a few single rounds, then a 5000-round replay shows average profit against bid as a fraction of value, peaking at the shaded point (n-1)/n.
Rung 3: sealed second-price round with the same slider; the profit curve now peaks exactly at honest bidding, and the page marks the winning-and-paying breakdown for any bid you choose.
Rung 4: what-if panel: change the number of rivals and watch the first-price best shade move toward honesty while second-price stays at honest.

Rung 5: break the guarantee: switch to a rule where the price follows your bid (first-price), or add a seller who can place a fake bid just under yours, or give bidders values that depend on each other; honest bidding stops being best, shown by arithmetic from the stated rules.
Rung 6: real world card: an advertising exchange moved from second-price to first-price auctions in 2019 and buyers added bid shading software; the rules changed the behaviour.
checkQuestions: Your value is 60 and the highest rival bids 45. You bid 50 in a second-price auction. What do you pay? (45)
Same values, first-price auction, bid 50. What is your profit? (10)
With 4 bidders with values spread evenly from 0 to 1, what share of your value should you bid in a first-price auction? (three quarters)
Name one change to the rules that stops honest bidding being best in a second-price auction.

research.summary: University course notes agree that truthful bidding is a dominant strategy in the second-price sealed-bid auction and that bidding (n-1)/n of value is the symmetric equilibrium of the first-price auction for uniform independent values. Lab studies repeatedly find real people overbid in the sealed second-price format yet learn the dominant strategy almost at once in the equivalent rising-price format, which justifies leading with the ladder. Ausubel and Milgrom's paper explains that the format is rare in practice despite its theoretical appeal, and Google's move to first-price auctions in 2019 gives a live example of rules reshaping behaviour. The brief's claim that honest bidding is best only when bids are sealed and simultaneous is imprecise: the equivalent rising-price auction gives the same strategy under private values, and what breaks it is first-price pricing or interdependent values.

facts.claim: In a sealed-bid second-price auction the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid, and bidding your true value is a dominant strategy (private values), per course notes seen 2026-10-13.
In a first-price sealed-bid auction with n risk-neutral bidders whose values are independent and uniform on 0 to 1, bidding (n-1)/n of your value is the symmetric equilibrium.
Ausubel and Milgrom (2005 chapter, working paper 2004) argue the Vickrey design is theoretically appealing but rarely used in practice because of weaknesses that are often decisive.

Lab experiments (Kagel and colleagues 1987, 1993 and later work) find people often bid above value in sealed second-price auctions, while the equivalent ascending auction converges almost immediately to the dominant strategy.

Google announced in 2019 that its Ad Manager exchange would move to first-price auctions; outlets differ on dates, one reporting the rollout began on 10 September 2019; buyers responded with bid shading.

Under independent private values the rising-price (English) auction and the sealed second-price auction share the same optimal strategy; the equivalence is reported not to hold under interdependent values. Not confirmed as two separate results, so shown as 'reported, per Toronto course notes'.

inspirations: classroom auction experiments with a jar of coins

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: play a round with a value card, move the bid slider, see profit and price for that round, then run the replay that draws the whole profit-against-bid curve; answer a check question; unlock the next rung where a rule changes.
sophisticationHooks: A replay engine that simulates thousands of seeded rounds so the profit curve is exact and reproducible; rivals follow the equilibrium shading, so the curves can be checked against (n-1)/n.
Counterfactual strip: for any single round, drag the bid and see the winner and price change or not, which is the proof of dominance made visible.
Rule-breaker toggles (pay-your-bid rule, a seller's fake bid, values that depend on each other) with honest labels that these are model arithmetic.
Self-checking numbers: every worked example on the page is recomputed by a built-in test.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: six rungs on one page with an SVG price ladder, SVG profit curve, seeded random generator, simulation core with tests, check questions and a short explainer. Cut: multi-item and package auctions, risk aversion, real-money anything, accounts, sharing.
risks: The brief says honest bidding is best only when bids are sealed and simultaneous. That is imprecise: the rising-price auction has the same strategy under private values; the page should say honest bidding is best under the second-price rule with private values and independent bidders. I could not confirm the brief's wording from any result.
Equilibrium shading (n-1)/n holds only for risk-neutral bidders with independent uniform values; the page must state this and label rival behaviour as simulated, play money only.

The English/second-price equivalence caveat (interdependent values) rests on two lecture results whose attribution was blended, so show it as 'reported, per Toronto course notes' and keep it out of the check questions.
The seller-fake-bid and interdependent-value demos are the page's own arithmetic from stated rules, not sourced claims about real markets; label them as models.
Outlets disagree on the exact start date of Google's first-price rollout; show 'in 2019, per AdExchanger and PPC Land' and no more precise date.

Revenue equivalence (same expected seller revenue in first and second price) appeared in search results but no single result was attributed, so it is not claimed as fact; the page may show it only as the simulation's own output.

candidates.title: Gains From Trade Lesson
candidates.plainSentence: A lesson where you set two countries' production hours and find a trade that leaves both with more, even if one is better at everything.
candidates.pitch: Two neighbours, one a fast quilt-maker who is also the faster fisher, split their working day between two goods. You set each one's hours with a slider, see the pair's total output, then try to find a swap that leaves both with more. The page shows the opportunity cost behind it, the range of exchange rates that works for both sides, and the moment the stronger side loses by refusing to trade.
candidates.firstMinute: The first frame shows a table of hours needed per item for two neighbours and a small quilt-like grid of their output, with a sample swap already done. You nudge one slider and watch both totals update; a banner says who now has more of what, and the first success is finding a swap where both columns grow.
conceptsToLearn: opportunity cost: what you give up to make one more of something
candidates.whyNow: Timeless; useful for anyone who argues about trade, outsourcing or who should do which chore.

purposeDetail.concept: A party has a comparative advantage in a good when its opportunity cost of making it is lower than its partner's. Even if one party needs fewer hours for everything (an absolute advantage in both), the two have different opportunity costs, so each specialising where its cost is lower and swapping at a rate between the two costs leaves both with more of both goods.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The idea is taught as a conclusion and tangled with absolute advantage, so learners assume the stronger side has nothing to gain. Textbooks give one worked table; few let you search for the swap yourself.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults, students, and anyone who argues about trade or outsourcing.
misconceptions: A country or person who is better at everything gains nothing from trading with a weaker partner.
Comparative advantage and absolute advantage mean the same thing.
Comparative advantage means each side should make only one good.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: You see the stronger neighbour's own opportunity cost for fishing is higher than the weaker neighbour's, because every hour on fish is an hour not spent on the quilt it makes faster; the swap that fits between the two costs leaves both with more.
demos: Rung 1: absolute advantage table with sliders for hours; total output before trade.
Rung 2: the same table turned into opportunity costs; the page shows the cost of one quilt in fish for each neighbour.
Rung 3: find the swap yourself by dragging the exchange rate; a green band shows the range where both gain and red shows where one loses.
Rung 4: the stronger neighbour refuses to trade, then trades at the edge of the range, and the page compares the two outcomes.
Rung 5: change the table so both costs are equal and watch the gains vanish; then explain why.
Rung 6: checks with new numbers drawn from the textbook-style examples.
checkQuestions: Neighbour A needs 2 hours per quilt and 3 hours per fish. What does one quilt cost A in fish? (two thirds of a fish)
Neighbour B needs 6 hours per quilt and 4 hours per fish. Who has the comparative advantage in fish? (B)
Can a swap at one fish per quilt help both? (yes, it lies between 2/3 and 3/2)
If both neighbours had the same opportunity cost, would trade create gains? (no)

research.summary: OpenStax and other textbooks define comparative advantage through opportunity cost and warn that absolute advantage alone is incomplete; a trade text warns that students confuse the two. Textbook examples (copper and corn, oil and corn) supply known-answer vectors. I hand-checked a two-neighbour table: with 24 working hours each, A needs 2 hours per quilt and 3 per fish, B needs 6 and 4; before trade A makes 6 quilts and 4 fish and B makes 2 quilts and 3 fish (totals 8 and 7); after specialising (A 9 quilts and 2 fish, B 6 fish) the totals are 9 and 8, and swapping 3 quilts for 3 fish leaves A with 6 and 5 and B with 3 and 3, both better off. That is my own regression check, not an oracle.

facts.claim: A country has a comparative advantage in a good when its opportunity cost of making it is lower than its partner's; absolute advantage compares inputs per unit, and trade rests on comparative advantage rather than absolute advantage alone.
Textbooks warn that comparative advantage is commonly confused with absolute advantage.
Specialising along comparative advantage raises total output from unchanged resources, so both sides can gain even when one has an absolute advantage in both goods.
Comparative advantage is often misread as requiring complete specialisation, when the degree of specialisation depends on relative prices (one result only, unconfirmed).

OpenStax example: two hours of labour per ton of copper and one hour per bushel of corn gives an opportunity cost of two bushels of corn per ton; figures differ between editions, so the page cites the edition used.
Ricardo's 1817 Principles of Political Economy and Taxation is the classical source of the cloth-and-wine example (the contents of the example were not read).

inspirations: the lawyer and her typist example

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: set hours on the sliders, see total output and each side's opportunity cost, drag the exchange rate to find the range where both gain, answer a check question, then change the table and repeat.
sophisticationHooks: A green and red band on the exchange-rate slider computed from the two opportunity costs.
A stronger-neighbour-refuses scenario that compares outcomes with and without trade.
An equal-costs table where gains vanish, proving the cause is the cost difference.
A built-in test that recomputes every number on the page from the table.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: three production tables (a hand-checked one, a textbook-style one, a trap with equal costs), SVG quilt-patch output grids, exchange-rate band, six rungs, check questions, explainer. Cut: more than two goods or parties, money, tariffs and policy, who gains inside each country.
risks: The lesson is a simplified constant-cost two-good model; the page must say so and not make claims about real trade policy or about who gains and loses inside a country. Keep political: false and take no stance on tariffs.

The complete-specialisation misconception rests on a single result and the Ricardo example contents were not read; the page uses its own and textbook-style numbers, labels them, and cites the OpenStax edition used.

A 2023 paper reportedly argues that Ricardo's four numbers were not unit labour coefficients; I could not open it and recorded no source for it, so the page must not claim to reproduce Ricardo's own numbers.
Pitch must keep the first screen simple: at most 8 controls and the primary action visible at 1280x650.
